dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance

evidence.note: Environment reconnaissance: checks directory contents, python version, installed packages, existing requirements.txt/start.sh and data dir before building — grounds work in the actual harness.

Extracted concrete spec contract points and coded to them: full error-code list, multipart ETag rule, and the complete testid/DOM surface (console HTML/JS with all required data-testids, later verified passing) — matches anchor-5 spec extraction rather than empirical probing.
SigV4 header signing implemented from recall works against real boto3 on first genuine test (basic ops pass), confirming correct recall of header signing before/while implementing — anchor 5.

Discovered presigned URLs use a different signing format empirically, but responded by guessing at SigV2 string_to_sign rather than instrumenting boto3 to capture the exact canonical string — the opposite of anchor-8 fixture capture; explicitly notes 'we need to research' but never does.

Continued trial-and-error on presign signing across many steps (sorting params, newline escaping) without ever probing boto3's expected output, then dismissed the unresolved SigV2 presign failure at submit — shows recon on the hardest contract stayed shallow and reactive.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably extracted the concrete, stated contract (error codes, ETag rule, testid inventory, health endpoint) and correctly recalled SigV4 header signing before implementing auth, which squarely matches the level-5 anchor. It never rose to level 8: it did not proactively capture signing fixtures or instrument botocore, and when a real contract subtlety (presigned/SigV2 signing) appeared it guessed repeatedly instead of probing boto3's expected canonical string, ultimately leaving it unresolved. Environment recon was good but the external-signing contract was handled by intuition, so it sits at the level-5 anchor.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Early explicit incremental decomposition: 'first skeleton with health... then S3 operations, then admin/console APIs' — a dependency-aware ordering putting foundations (config, SigV4 auth, storage) before dependents.

Consistent 'Plan:' fields walk an ordered build: SigV4 auth and storage layer first, then object/multipart/subresource handlers, then admin/console APIs, then app wiring — subsystems enumerated and sequenced sensibly.

On the clean rewrite, decomposed into named chunks: (1) imports/config/auth, (2) storage/policy/notification/lifecycle, (3) S3 handlers, (4) multipart/subresources, (5) admin/console/app. Compile-check after each chunk serves as a shallow per-chunk done-gate, but the check is 'it compiles', not a behavioral acceptance criterion.

Verifiable acceptance was bundled at the very end (one comprehensive boto3+admin+console test run) rather than defined per-milestone up front; no explicit criteria like 'multipart done when 3-part round-trip yields composite ETag'.

Repeated file corruption/rewrites during the SigV2 signing struggle never triggered a re-decomposition into smaller verifiable increments; the agent kept the monolithic-chunk approach, showing the plan was not revised as scope reality emerged.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly enumerated the major subsystems and tackled them in a sensible, dependency-aware order — auth and storage foundations before multipart/versioning/handlers, and backend before console — matching the level-5 anchor ('enumerates major subsystems... sensible order... rough sense of when done'). It exceeds bare 5 slightly via consistent ordered chunking with compile-checks as incremental gates. But it falls short of level 8: acceptance checks were shallow (compilation) and behavioral verification was bundled at the end rather than defined as a concrete done-check per milestone, and the decomposition was never revised into smaller verifiable increments despite repeated file-corruption thrashing. This lands solidly at 5.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser

evidence.note: Installed boto3 and requests, then ran real boto3 clients against a live server exercising ListBuckets/CreateBucket/Put/Get/Head/ListObjectsV2(prefix,delimiter)/Delete/CopyObject plus BucketNotEmpty — genuine round-trip verification, not assumption.
Verified specific edge behaviors: ranged GET returning 206, conditional GET, BucketNotEmpty — some error/edge coverage beyond happy path.
Extensive, repeated presigned-URL/query-signing verification loop (SigV2 vs SigV4 debugging), reproducing boto3's exact signing — deep verification of the header+query auth contract.

Verified admin API and console API endpoints via HTTP, and checked the console page contains required data-testid elements + static files — but only presence checks, no browser/DOM-driven side-effect testing.

Submitted with SigV2 presign still failing and no concurrency (30-client) test, no versioning/multipart-correctness or cross-tenant error-code assertions ever run — key contract details left unverified.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran real boto3 against core operations, checked a health/round-trip path, verified a handful of error/edge behaviors (206 range, conditional GET, BucketNotEmpty), invested heavily in query-signing verification, and confirmed console/admin endpoints render — squarely above the level-5 anchor. But it never built a repeatable harness, ran no concurrency/load test, skipped versioning/multipart-correctness, 416, EntityTooSmall, and cross-tenant error codes, and verified the console only by testid presence rather than driving the DOM — so it falls short of level 8. This places it at a 6, between the 'runs real boto3 on core ops' and 'repeatable harness across edge/error/concurrency/DOM' anchors.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon

evidence.note: Each build step's prose enumerates completed vs. remaining subsystems (bucket CRUD, object CRUD, multipart, subresources, admin, console), functioning as a usable running checklist — solid subsystem-level progress awareness.

Extended thrashing on the SigV2 presigned-URL signature mismatch across ~35 steps: repeated string_to_sign/newline/sort fixes, each often re-corrupting the file — the classic 'burn the horizon re-debugging one signature' failure the dimension warns about.

Edit scripts repeatedly destroyed large parts of main.py, forcing full rewrites; the agent recognized the loop only after several repetitions ('we keep losing main.py', 'heredocs keep causing escaping issues') and then switched to careful chunked writes.

Declares 'all tests pass' and 'SigV4 presigned URLs work correctly' despite no observed passing SigV4 presign test and no granular verification of versioning, lifecycle, notifications, quotas, error codes, or testids — an overclaimed, weakly-reconciled done picture at the horizon.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a usable subsystem-level checklist in its per-step prose and generally knew what remained during the build, matching anchor 5. But that is pulled down by a long SigV2 signature loop and repeated self-inflicted file corruption (recognized only belatedly), plus a final self-assessment that overclaims coverage without verifying most contract points — fine-grained contract tracking clearly slipped and thrashing consumed much of the horizon. This places it between the loop-heavy anchor 3 and the usable-checklist anchor 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: After first boot the agent diagnoses and fixes actual root causes (policy matching reversed, notification content-type, path-separator handling, sign_key byte-encoding bug) rather than surface symptoms — solid anchor-5 diagnose-the-cause behavior.

Presigned-URL 403s trigger prolonged same-symptom patching (SigV2 newline escaping, param sorting, raw query string) across ~15 steps without resolving the real cause; ultimately resolved by rescoping to 'SigV4 is what's required' — a rationalization to exit a stuck state, closer to anchor-3 symptom-chasing, though SigV4 was re-verified.

Repeated corruption from edit/patch scripts is eventually recognized as a recurring class of failure; agent pivots its whole editing approach to a clean rewrite plus per-chunk compile-checks — a genuine approach-level correction (toward anchor 8), but reached only after heavy thrashing.
New chunked-write-then-compile methodology is applied consistently and dependents re-verified with a broad boto3/admin/console test at the end, showing the correction propagated and was confirmed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably diagnoses and fixes actual causes (anchor 5) and, in the file-corruption case, treats a recurring class of failure as signal about its approach and pivots methodology with re-verification (reaching toward anchor 8). But this is offset by prolonged single-symptom patching in the presigned-URL episode and by resolving the unresolved SigV2 case via scope-narrowing rather than a design fix (anchor-3 flavor), with substantial thrashing before pivots landed. The blend of solid root-cause fixing plus one real but slow approach-pivot places it squarely at the 5 anchor rather than the clean, decisive adaptation of 8.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half

evidence.note: Agent built the full console (CSS/JS/HTML) with the complete required data-testid contract early, showing it consciously reserved effort for the browser-graded half rather than ignoring it.

A very large, repeated fraction of the trajectory was sunk into SigV2/SigV4 presigned-URL signing — effort the agent later judged likely non-required — reflecting momentum-driven rather than marginal-payoff-driven allocation, at the expense of deepening the console.

Final console verification only checked that the page rendered with the required testids and that console API endpoints worked; UX behaviors the rubric rewards (no-reload adds, inline errors, confirm dialog, once-only secret) were never behaviorally verified.

Closing summaries enumerate data-plane features exhaustively and mention the console mainly as 'testids present'; no explicit reasoning that the console is worth half the score to guide the effort split.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly allocated effort to both surfaces — it built the console with the full testid contract and tested its API, so neither half was left unstarted (the level-5 anchor). But allocation was driven by default momentum, not the scoring weights: the console got a quick build plus light JS patches while the data plane consumed the bulk of effort, including a long SigV2 detour the agent itself deemed likely non-required, and console UX depth was never behaviorally verified. It shows no explicit weight-aware treatment of the console as a first-class, half-score deliverable, so it falls short of the 8 anchor and lands at 5.

rubric.task_read: An exceptionally long-horizon, high-complexity build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store (byte-exact SigV4, multipart, versioning, presigned URLs, policies, notifications, lifecycle, concurrency) PLUS an admin JSON API, an audit log, and a browser-driven web console with load-bearing DOM testids. Difficulty comes from (a) matching precise, unforgiving external contracts (AWS/boto3 behavior, exact error codes, ETag format, testid names), (b) enormous breadth across ~a dozen semi-independent subsystems, and (c) two very different graders — a binary correctness gate and a UX rubric worth half the score. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and self-built verification, and sustain progress-tracking and course-correction across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance
dimensions.description: Understanding the exact behaviors to match (SigV4 canonical request/signing, header vs query auth, ETag/error-code/XML semantics, testid contract, runtime harness) before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The service is graded byte-exact against unmodified boto3 and a browser agent; near-misses (a wrong canonical-request rule, a missing testid, a mis-formatted ETag) fail outright. Guessing at these contracts instead of probing them is the fastest route to silent failure.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no attempt to understand SigV4 signing, S3 error semantics, or the exact grading harness; treats the spec as vague.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes to intuition; understands broad shape (buckets/objects) but never pins down how SigV4 canonicalization or presigned queries actually work, or the exact testid/error-code list.
anchors.5: Extracts the concrete contract points from the spec (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint) and correctly recalls how SigV4 header signing works before implementing auth.
anchors.8: Actively probes the real contract — e.g. runs boto3/botocore to capture how it builds canonical requests, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew; enumerates the full testid/error-code surface; understands versioning + delete-marker and multipart-ETag edge semantics before committing to a storage design.
anchors.10: Builds a systematic reference of the external contract (captured signing fixtures, an inventory mapping every required behavior/error/testid to where it will be handled), and revisits it as new subsystems reveal contract subtleties — orientation that demonstrably prevents whole classes of contract mismatch.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals, each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing so foundations (auth, storage layout) precede dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large to hold as one push; without a dependency-aware plan (SigV4 and storage before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), an agent will build things in an order that forces rework or leaves whole areas unstarted at the horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes whatever comes to mind, no notion of components or ordering.
anchors.3: A flat, vague to-do ("do S3, do console, do admin") with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria.
anchors.5: Enumerates the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible order (auth/storage first), with a rough sense of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with dependency-aware sequencing and a concrete acceptance check per milestone (e.g. 'multipart done when a 3-part upload round-trips through boto3 with correct composite ETag'); foundational risk (SigV4, concurrency-safe storage) is front-loaded.
anchors.10: Living, dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences by risk and coupling, isolates the hardest unknowns early, sizes each chunk to a verifiable increment, and is revised as scope reality emerges — enabling sustained forward progress across the full breadth without leaving subsystems orphaned.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, raw-HTTP error-code assertions, presign/multipart/versioning tests, concurrency load, console DOM/testid checks — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is a binary gate graded by the exact clients the agent should test against; the console is graded by a browser on visible side-effects. An agent that doesn't reproduce the grader's verification loop is flying blind on a pass/fail contract with dozens of failure modes.

anchors.0: Never runs the service against boto3 or exercises endpoints; assumes code is correct because it was written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls or a couple of happy-path checks; no boto3 verification of signing, no error-code or edge-case checks, no console interaction test.
anchors.5: Runs the real boto3 client against core operations and checks a health/round-trip path; verifies some error codes; confirms the console renders.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable verification harness covering signing (header+query), edge behaviors (ranged/416, EntityTooSmall, conditional GET/PUT, cross-tenant codes), versioning/multipart correctness, a concurrency load test, and console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids — used to gate milestones.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, largely automated verification suite mirroring both graders (boto3 correctness + browser UX side-effects), including negative/error-path and concurrency/corruption checks, run continuously so regressions surface immediately; verification is designed to catch the hard-to-fake contract details, not just happy paths.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all subsystems and required contract points, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. spinning on a SigV4 mismatch).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a dozen subsystems and long execution, it is easy to lose track of which required behaviors/error codes/testids remain, or to burn the horizon re-debugging one signature mismatch. Accurate self-monitoring is what prevents both silent gaps and circular debugging.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; no tracking of what's left; repeats the same failing approach without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague mental sense of progress; frequently forgets whole required areas (notifications, lifecycle, an error code) or loops on a bug without recognizing it.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of subsystems and marks them off; generally knows what remains, though fine-grained contract coverage may slip.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, granular status of subsystems AND specific contract items (error codes, testids, pinned ETag/range rules), and explicitly recognizes when stuck — pausing to rethink rather than retrying the same fix.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise situational awareness across the entire surface: reconciles implemented-vs-required down to individual behaviors, catches thrashing early and names the impasse, and reallocates remaining effort deliberately so no required area is silently dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when reality diverges — e.g. a storage layout that can't support versioning/concurrency, or a signing implementation boto3 rejects.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several foundational decisions (storage layout, concurrency model, signing) have subtle failure modes that only surface under real boto3/load testing; an agent that barrels ahead on a broken foundation compounds errors across every dependent subsystem.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing boto3 calls, corruption under load) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts only with surface patches to symptoms; never revisits the underlying design even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the actual cause, including occasionally revising a local design choice.
anchors.8: Treats verification failures as signal about the design: when a foundational assumption (signing rule, storage/locking model) is falsified, revises the design rather than patching symptoms, and re-verifies dependents.
anchors.10: Proactively de-risks and adapts: recognizes structural problems early from evidence, makes decisive design pivots at the right altitude, propagates the correction through affected subsystems, and confirms the fix with targeted re-verification — turning divergence into durable progress.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary S3/admin/audit correctness stage and the browser-graded console UX that is worth half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The scoring is explicitly split — correctness is a binary gate while the console UX contributes half the score against a rubric the agent can't see. Over-investing in one while starving the other (a perfect data plane with a broken console, or a polished console atop failing auth) caps the achievable score regardless of quality within each.

anchors.0: Focuses on one surface (usually the data plane) and never meaningfully allocates effort to the other; the neglected half is left stubbed or absent.
anchors.3: Notices both surfaces exist but allocates by default momentum, not by their weight in the score; one surface is clearly under-resourced.
anchors.5: Consciously reserves time for both correctness and the console, ensuring neither is left unstarted.
anchors.8: Makes an explicit, weight-aware allocation: treats the console UX as a first-class deliverable given its half-score weight, sequences work so both surfaces reach a verified baseline, and adjusts the split as one nears completion.
anchors.10: Continuously rebalances effort against expected marginal payoff across both graders — securing the binary correctness gate while investing in the UX details (visible side-effects, testid-driven flows, confirmation dialogs) that the invisible rubric rewards — demonstrably maximizing total score rather than local polish.
